article_title: Effects of an International Undergraduate Honors Course on Awareness of Global Justice
citation: Ingrid Schutte, Elanor Kamans, Marca Wolfensberger and Wiel Veugelers. (2018). Effects of an International Undergraduate Honors Course on Awareness of Global Justice. Educ. Sci. 2018, 8, 82. https://doi.org/10.3390/educsci8020082
title: Curriculum guidelines for global justice citizenship education (GJCE)
description: The GJCE guidelines organize global citizenship education around three intertwined domains: knowledge, attitude and values, and a pedagogical approach. Knowledge means that "Knowledge provides the basis for insight into global justice issues and their root causes", with deep knowledge built from a focus on one global issue, historical insight, and local–global relationships. Attitude and values cover ethical and intercultural sensitivity, contact with people from different backgrounds, and critical reflection on mainstream thinking. The pedagogical approach centers on experiential learning in civic contexts. The authors used the guidelines both to analyze the SIS course program and to structure the case study's outcome measures.
requirements: Spend at least 15 h in civic contexts
Focus on one global-justice issue with historical insight into root causes and local–global connections
Develop ethical and intercultural sensitivity and critically reflect on mainstream thinking
constraints: The guidelines were developed simultaneously but largely independently of the SIS course, so the case study could not fully assess their value for preparing students for global justice citizenship

The SIS course lacked deep knowledge of one issue, historical insight into root causes, and critical reflection on mainstream values, and was characterized as soft rather than critical global citizenship
target_learners: Undergraduate honors students in higher education
target_learning_goals: Insight into root causes of global justice issues
Motivation and possibilities to take action for a more just society
examples: The SIS course strongly implemented contact with people from different cultural and socio-economic backgrounds, intercultural cooperation, and experiential learning with 25% of class time in the community interviewing migrants, while covering one global issue, historical insights, and value reflection only partially

article_title: Integrating the Triple Jump Exercise and gamification (G-Jump) to enhance learning outcomes among anesthesia students: a preliminary quasi-experimental study.
citation: Jafarpoor Hasanali, Falavarjani Hossein Ghasemi, Shokrani Amirhossein, Mortazavi Yosef, Kazemzadeh Asal, Darzi Fatemeh Hasaninejad, Behnam Fatemeh. (2026). Integrating the Triple Jump Exercise and gamification (G-Jump) to enhance learning outcomes among anesthesia students: a preliminary quasi-experimental study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-08933-1
title: G-Jump: a three-stage gamified Triple Jump Exercise assessment model for anesthesia education
description: G-Jump integrates the Triple Jump Exercise with gamification following the Werbach–Hunter framework. Its three jumps are a points-based competitive closed-book case MCQ test, an open-book case analysis scored for response quality and search strategy, and a structured reflective narrative scored by two evaluators (inter-rater reliability ICC = 0.87). Game elements include a "Plague Doctor" narrative, live leaderboards, badges, and real-time feedback. The study evaluated it against TJE and closed-book control in a three-group quasi-experiment.
requirements: Students received a detailed guidebook and attended an orientation session to ensure familiarity with the process
requires an eight-member expert panel spanning medical education, anesthesiology, and instructional design
constraints: Implementation complexity — including design, training, and evaluation — may challenge large-scale adoption
target_learners: undergraduate anesthesia students in health profession education
target_learning_goals: information search, analysis, and synthesis skills
examples: Students answered case-based MCQs in a competitive, points-based format with live leaderboard updates and a Badge of Excellence for scoring ≥ 60 points
Second jump participants analyzed simulated clinical cases using online resources, with badge holders receiving general hints to preserve fairness

article_title: Integrating the Triple Jump Exercise and gamification (G-Jump) to enhance learning outcomes among anesthesia students: a preliminary quasi-experimental study.
citation: Jafarpoor Hasanali, Falavarjani Hossein Ghasemi, Shokrani Amirhossein, Mortazavi Yosef, Kazemzadeh Asal, Darzi Fatemeh Hasaninejad, Behnam Fatemeh. (2026). Integrating the Triple Jump Exercise and gamification (G-Jump) to enhance learning outcomes among anesthesia students: a preliminary quasi-experimental study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-08933-1
title: G-Jump framework grounded in Self-Determination and Flow theories with self-referenced progress over peer rivalry
description: The article grounds the G-Jump framework theoretically in Self-Determination and Flow theories. It holds that gamified assessment fosters intrinsic motivation by satisfying needs for autonomy through self-paced progression and competence via immediate feedback, while maintaining an optimal balance between task challenge and student skill level to prevent cognitive overload and facilitate flow. Design choices also align with Nicol and Macfarlane-Dick's model of formative feedback as a motivational mechanism supporting self-regulation.
requirements: the design must prioritize "self-referenced progress over peer rivalry" to mitigate risks of unhealthy competition or psychological stress
constraints: the potential "novelty effect" must be acknowledged; the article states longitudinal research is required to determine whether high engagement persists once gamified assessment becomes routine
examples: Narrative and aesthetic elements, consistent visual design, immersive storytelling, and real-time narrative feedback were used to sustain attention and emotional involvement
